newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade official sees steady surplus decline.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade official sees steady surplus decline.

text.p: A robust appetite for imports means Japan's trade surplus is likely to keep falling steadily, though less rapidly than in the recent past, a senior Japanese trade official said on Tuesday.
"You can have several different scenarios," Hisashi Hosokawa, vice minister for international affairs at the Ministry of International Trade and Industry, told Reuters in an interview.
"But my own prediction is the...continued, steady decline of the trade surplus."

Hosokawa, who assumed his post as Japan's top international trade bureaucrat earlier this month, said the pace of the decline in the trade surplus would slow, but denied that a weaker yen was making Japanese exports more competitive.

"There will be a steady decline, but not a sharp decline. That does not mean at all that because of the weakened yen, Japanese exports are rising," he said, adding that structural changes in Japan's economy would continue to boost imports.
"Japanese imports...are really increasing and this trend will not be changing," he said.

Japan's latest monthly trade data showed that the nation's trade surplus dropped almost 38 percent to 504.03 billion yen ($4.66 billion) in July when compared to the previous year -- the 20th consecutive month of year-on-year declines.
Economists said, however, that a four percent rise in export volume heralded moderate export growth for the rest of the year.

Hosokawa said Japanese firms appeared to welcome the recent stability in the foreign exchange market, although he declined to comment on the desirability of any specific currency level. "People engaging in real business seem to be happy with the stable market situation," he said.

Commenting on a dispute over U.S. allegations of unfair practices in Japan's consumer photo film and paper market, which Washington took to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) earlier this year, Hosokawa said Tokyo was prepared to accept whatever ruling the Geneva-based global trade body made -- and believed the United States would do the same.

Washington earlier this month requested two WTO dispute-settlement panels after consultations with Tokyo failed to make progress in resolving the dispute centring on Eastman Kodak Co's complaints over access to Japan's market.
"All member countries are supposed to respect panel decisions and neither Japan nor the United States, hopefully, is an exception," he said.

Hosokawa said U.S. and Japanese officials would likely meet next month to review a two-way pact on automotive trade forged last year, and rejected recent complaints by U.S. Secretary of Commerce Mickey Kantor that Japan was not honouring its obligations under the agreement.
When the deal was forged last year, Washington announced its own numerical forecasts for car and car parts trade, while Tokyo simultaneously disowned the numbers.
"The Japanese government, particularly MITI, was very quick to point out that that (Kantor's comment) was not a correct interpretation of the agreed text," Hosokawa said.
Hosokawa, a graduate of Harvard's John F. Kennedy School of Government who speaks fluent English, said he would make his first overseas visit as vice minister to the United States next week.
He plans to meet businessmen, academics and U.S. officials, including possibly Ira Shapiro, senior negotiator at the U.S. Trade Representative's office. ($1=108 yen)
